findings.title: 'Jesus' prefix on cosmic wisdom entities is Manichaean-Christian overlay
findings.current_state: The text consistently names two distinct cosmic entities 'Jesus the Splendour' and 'Jesus the Youth.' E.g. §27: 'The fourth day is Jesus the Splendour'; §377: 'Jesus the Youth was set there; who is the image of the living word.'
findings.explanation: These are the most clearly overlaid names in the corpus. 'Jesus the Splendour' (Isho' Ziwa) and 'Jesus the Youth' are specifically Manichaean designations mapped onto cosmic entities that the substrate described as principles of illuminating wisdom and the first revelation of divine truth. The epithet 'the Splendour' (Syriac Zīwā) maps to Iranian xvarənah/farr (divine radiance/glory) and is likely substrate. But the 'Jesus' prefix is Mani's editorial identification of this cosmic figure with Jesus of Nazareth — a mapping absent from the pre-Manichaean Persian teaching. The substrate would have used 'the Splendour' alone, or paired the epithet with a Persian divine name. The entity functions throughout as the fourth proceeding of the Divine (§73: 'The third originating degree... he is glorious Jesus the Splendour'), as the one who illuminates and separates truth from falsity (§42, §160–162, §184, §291), and as the image of living truth (§377). None of these functions require the 'Jesus' identification; all are fulfilled by a cosmic wisdom principle known in Iranian tradition.
findings.recommendation: Flag 'Jesus' as editorial prefix throughout. The substrate name was most probably 'the Splendour' (Zīwā/Farr) alone, or possibly a Persian divine name such as a form of Sraosha or a Zurvanite wisdom-entity. Retain the epithets 'the Splendour' and 'the Youth' as likely substrate. Where the text reads 'Jesus the Splendour,' the substrate likely read 'the Splendour' or '[Persian name] the Splendour.'

findings.title: 'Saklas and his consort' is Gnostic (Sethian) naming, not substrate
findings.current_state: §592: 'All these abortions, amongst them are Saklas and his consort and the ones whom they have served'
findings.explanation: 'Saklas' (from Aramaic/Hebrew sakhla = fool) is a Gnostic demiurge name from the Sethian tradition, specifically from texts like the Apocryphon of John. This name has no roots in Persian or Zurvanite cosmology. The substrate entity — the chief ruler of the abortive cosmic productions who fashioned Adam and Eve — would have been named with a Persian designation, likely related to the Zurvanite concept of Ahriman's chief demon or a functional epithet describing the 'chief of the malformed ones.' The Gnostic naming here reflects the Coptic-Egyptian milieu of the Kephalaia's compilation, not the Persian substrate.
findings.recommendation: Flag 'Saklas' as Gnostic overlay. The substrate likely used a Persian demiurge name or functional description such as 'the chief of the malformed ones' or 'the ruler of the abortions.' Investigate whether a Zurvanite demon name (perhaps Kūndag or a derivative of Ahriman's lieutenants) would fit the substrate's cosmological position.

findings.title: 'Cross of Light' and 'crucified' in cosmic contexts are Manichaean-Christian vocabulary overlaying a substrate concept
findings.current_state: §4: 'He crucified it in [...]'; §32: 'which the Living Spirit crucified in the universe'; §394: 'the living soul... is like the Cross of Light'; §703: 'this Light Cross that is established in silence'
findings.explanation: The Manichaean 'Cross of Light' (σταυρός τοῦ φωτός) and the verb 'crucified' in cosmic contexts are Mani's mapping of Christian crucifixion imagery onto the substrate concept of divine elements scattered, stretched, and bound throughout creation. The substrate teaching — that wisdom is dispersed and held captive within the natural order — is clearly pre-Christian and appears in Zurvanite cosmology as the binding or mixing (gumēzišn) of light with darkness. The verb 'crucified' in §4, §32, §35, §327 describes cosmic binding/stretching, not historical crucifixion. The substrate likely used a Persian verb meaning 'bound,' 'stretched out,' or 'affixed' (cf. Middle Persian band- or āwēxt-). The term 'Cross of Light' in §394, §640, §694, §703, §771, §773 names a genuine substrate concept — the suffering divine presence within matter — but the word 'Cross' (σταυρός) is the Manichaean-Christian designation.
findings.recommendation: Flag 'crucified' and 'Cross of Light' as Manichaean-Christian vocabulary. The substrate concept is authentic (scattered/bound divine elements), but the terminology is editorial. The substrate likely used terms meaning 'bound throughout,' 'stretched and affixed,' or 'the suffering of wisdom' (cf. Zurvanite gumēzišn). Retain the concept; flag the specific vocabulary as overlay.

findings.title: 'Matter' (Hylē) as personified feminine entity is Greek philosophical overlay on Persian Āz/Jeh
findings.current_state: §31: 'Matter, the sculptress'; §32: 'she, this Matter, the thought of death'; §52: 'Matter, who is the thought of death, the one who sculpted him'; §252: 'this Matter, this thought of Death'
findings.explanation: The personified feminine entity consistently called 'Matter' (Coptic rendering of Greek ὕλη) throughout the corpus is the Manichaean philosophical name for a figure the substrate described with a Persian designation. The consistent substrate epithet 'the thought of death' is preserved alongside 'Matter,' suggesting the editorial pattern: [Persian name] → 'Matter' while 'the thought of death' was retained as a gloss. In Zurvanite tradition, this figure corresponds to Āz (concupiscence/greed — the feminine demon who animates the forces of darkness) or Jeh (the demonic feminine who seduces and fashions). The entity's functions in the substrate — fashioning the corporeal world (§31: 'the sculptress'), giving strength to the forces of evil for war (§32), being the 'mother of all' evil forms (§35) — align precisely with Āz/Jeh in the Bundahišn and Zurvanite sources. The Greek philosophical abstraction 'Matter' obscures the vivid Persian mythological character.
findings.recommendation: Flag 'Matter' as Greek-Manichaean philosophical overlay. The substrate name was most probably Āz (concupiscence/greed) or Jeh, a personified feminine evil principle in Zurvanite cosmology. The epithet 'the thought of death' appears to be genuine substrate retained alongside the editorial name. Consider restoring the reading: 'Āz, the thought of death' or 'Jeh, the thought of death.'

findings.title: 'Holy Spirit' is Christian terminology replacing substrate 'Great Spirit' or 'Living Spirit'
findings.current_state: §427: 'they have blasphemed and despised the Holy Spirit since every generation of the world'; §617: 'The Holy Spirit reigns. It does all that it pleases.'
findings.explanation: The term 'Holy Spirit' appears only twice in the entire extracted corpus, while the substrate consistently uses 'Great Spirit' (§65, §112, §141, §158, §286, §907) and 'Living Spirit' (§5, §101, §109, §116, etc.) for related divine proceeding entities. 'Holy Spirit' is specifically Christian theological vocabulary that was not caught by the extraction pipeline. In §427, the phrase 'blasphemed and despised the Holy Spirit' echoes Mark 3:29 / Matthew 12:31 (the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit) — a distinctly Pauline/Synoptic formulation. In §617, 'The Holy Spirit reigns' replaces what the substrate's own terminology would render as 'The Great Spirit reigns' or 'The Living Spirit reigns,' consistent with the teaching's established vocabulary. Both instances represent Christian editorial vocabulary that slipped through extraction.
findings.recommendation: Flag both instances for restoration to substrate vocabulary. §427: 'the Great Spirit' (consistent with §65, §112, §286). §617: 'the Living Spirit' or 'the Great Spirit' (consistent with the surrounding teaching context where the Light Mind and the Living Spirit are the active divine agents). The Pauline echo in §427 ('blasphemed the Holy Spirit') should be noted as a particularly clear case of Christian editorial contamination.

findings.title: 'Second death' is Christian eschatological vocabulary from Revelation
findings.current_state: §428: 'the second death is eternal. It is the second death!'
findings.explanation: The phrase 'second death' (δεύτερος θάνατος) is a distinctly Christian eschatological term appearing in Revelation 2:11, 20:6, 20:14, 21:8. While the substrate clearly teaches a concept of eternal spiritual death contrasted with temporal spiritual death (the entire §414–§428 passage distinguishes the two), the specific designation 'second death' is Johannine-Christian vocabulary imposed by the editorial layer. The exclamatory repetition 'It is the second death!' has a distinctly homiletic/devotional quality characteristic of later editorial expansion. The substrate would have used a more descriptive Persian designation — perhaps 'the eternal death' or 'the death without end' — consistent with Zurvanite eschatological vocabulary about the final fate of evil.
findings.recommendation: Flag 'second death' as Christian editorial vocabulary. The underlying teaching about two forms of spiritual death (temporal vs. eternal) appears to be genuine substrate, but the specific phrase is overlay from Revelation. Consider whether the substrate read 'the eternal death' or 'the death from which there is no returning' — a formulation more consistent with §14's 'they have no repentance therein' and §17's 'until he arrives at the [lump],' both of which express the same concept without Christian vocabulary.

findings.title: Audience frame material preserved as core: 'There are some among us telling us...'
findings.current_state: §577: 'There are some among us telling us that we [know and perceive] that the (Ambassador) consents about [that] figure of flesh...'
findings.explanation: This paragraph opens with 'There are some among us telling us...' which is an audience objection formula — a community member raising a theological concern to the teacher. This is editorial frame material: it establishes the Manichaean community context ('among us'), voices an internal debate, and sets up the teaching response (§578–§583). The teaching response itself (§578–§583) is clearly substrate — it contains the cosmological explanation of how the Ambassador's image was displayed and the rulers fashioned Adam after it. But §577's opening frame belongs to the Manichaean institutional layer. In other chapters, such audience questions and objections appear to have been properly stripped. The teaching in §578 begins naturally with 'Regarding the Ambassador...' and would flow directly from the preceding cosmological material without §577.
findings.recommendation: Flag §577 as frame material that should have been stripped or classified as MIXED. The opening formula 'There are some among us telling us...' is institutional. The substantive theological content of the objection (about whether the Ambassador 'consents' to the formation of flesh) may contain substrate elements, but the framing is editorial. Consider reclassifying §577 as FRAME and letting §578 begin the teaching response directly.

findings.title: 'Light Mind' (Nous) is Greek-Manichaean terminology throughout
findings.current_state: §74: 'The first power whom he summoned is the Light Mind'; §366: 'the Light Mind is this one who shall come and assume the saints'; §390: 'until the Light Mind finds how to humble this body'
findings.explanation: The entity called 'Light Mind' (φωτεινὸς νοῦς) appears throughout the corpus as a major cosmic figure — the divine intelligence that enters the regenerating person, binds the old man, forms the new man, and governs the faculties (§366–§413). The term 'Nous' is Greek philosophical vocabulary (from Neoplatonic and Hermetic traditions) that Mani adopted. The substrate entity — the divine intelligence that illuminates the human understanding — would have been designated with a Persian term. In Zoroastrian tradition, this maps to Vohu Manah (Good Mind/Good Thought), one of the Amesha Spentas, whose function — to enter the righteous person and awaken divine understanding — precisely parallels the Light Mind's role throughout §366–§413. The Greek 'Nous' obscures this Iranian heritage.
findings.recommendation: Flag 'Light Mind' as Manichaean-Greek nomenclature. The substrate designation was most probably Vohu Manah (Good Mind/Good Thought) or a Zurvanite equivalent. The entire §366–§413 passage about the Light Mind entering the body, binding the old man, and forming the new man corresponds precisely to Zoroastrian teachings about Vohu Manah's role in the soul. Consider noting this correspondence in future restoration work.

findings.title: 'The elect one' is Manichaean institutional vocabulary
findings.current_state: §106: 'the heart of the elect one, who is come forth from his body'; §413: 'He bestows a great spirit upon the elect one'
findings.explanation: 'The elect' (electi) is a technical term for the higher grade of Manichaean practitioner, distinguished from 'hearers' (auditores/catechumens). This institutional vocabulary was not caught by the extraction pipeline. The substrate would have used a functional description — perhaps 'the purified one,' 'the righteous one,' or 'the one who has separated' — consistent with the teaching's own themes of discrimination and purification. The use in §106 (describing the soul's departure from the body) and §413 (describing the bestowal of spiritual power) does not require institutional categories.
findings.recommendation: Flag 'the elect one' for replacement with a functional substrate term. 'The purified one' or 'the one who has distinguished [good from evil]' would be consistent with the teaching's own vocabulary about discrimination (§16–§17) and purification.

findings.title: 'Church tutelaries' is institutional vocabulary with uncertain meaning
findings.current_state: §95: 'all of them also, and the church tutelaries (?), and the kinsfolk who belong to the household of his people'
findings.explanation: The phrase 'church tutelaries (?)' contains institutional vocabulary ('church') and the translator's own uncertainty marker (?). The term appears to refer to guardian figures associated with an institutional community. The substrate would have described these as guardian spirits, protective heavenly beings, or household gods (a concept natural to the Persian-Iranian religious context). The word 'church' (ἐκκλησία) is a Christian-institutional term that does not belong in the substrate layer.
findings.recommendation: Flag 'church tutelaries' as editorial. The substrate likely read something like 'the guardian spirits' or 'the protective beings of the household' — a functional description consistent with the surrounding context about gods, angels, and kinsfolk of the celestial community.

findings.title: Numbered objections retained as core in §367–§370 but similar frame questions stripped elsewhere
findings.current_state: §367: 'So, now, where is he?'; §368: 'If then he is a great God...'; §369: 'Thirdly a holy one is the Mind...'; §370: 'Fourthly: If truly the Light Mind exists in the saints...'
findings.explanation: These four paragraphs present numbered objections (explicitly 'Thirdly,' 'Fourthly') that set up the teaching response about the Light Mind in the body (§371ff). They function as frame material — questions posed to the teacher that establish the pedagogical context. In other chapters, such question-and-answer formulas appear to have been stripped (e.g., the chapter boundaries generally begin with the teaching content rather than the introductory questions). The retention here may be justified if these objections are considered integral to the substrate's own dialectical teaching method, but the numbered format ('Thirdly,' 'Fourthly') implies they belong to a structured Q&A session rather than to the flowing teaching narrative. The inconsistency should be noted.
findings.recommendation: Review §367–§370 for reclassification. If other chapters consistently strip Q&A formulas, these should be reclassified as FRAME or MIXED. If the substrate's own teaching method includes dialectical objections, they should be retained — but then similar passages in other chapters should be checked for consistency.

findings.title: Five-fold architecture is the universal structural principle of the entire corpus
findings.current_state: The number five governs every teaching sequence: five elements (§48), five limbs/faculties (§11, §14, §202, §322, §395), five garments/sons (§230, §557–§560), five fathers (§63–§83), five wars (§179–§185), five releases (§186–§197), five greatnesses (§138–§145), five hunters (§39–§47), five signs (§91–§106), five camps (§729–§734), five storehouses (§48), five dens (§849), five productions (§858–§863), five emanations from five limbs (§265–§266), twenty-five as five-times-five (§878).
findings.explanation: The five-fold structure is not merely recurrent but architectonic — it IS the substrate's organizing principle. Every teaching sequence, whether describing the divine realm, the infernal realm, the human body, the cosmic order, or the process of regeneration, deploys a five-fold pattern. This is visible only at corpus scale. The five-fold pattern corresponds to the Zoroastrian Amesha Spentas (six in Zoroastrian tradition, but five when the supreme deity is excluded from the count — precisely the pattern here where the Father/First stands apart and the five proceed from him). The substrate's five-fold architecture is the Persian correspondential equivalent of what Swedenborg describes as discrete degrees — but organized around five rather than three. The deeper question (for further study) is whether this five-fold pattern represents a pre-Zoroastrian Indo-Iranian template that the Zoroastrian tradition later modified into its hexad.
findings.recommendation: Treat the five-fold pattern as the primary structural key for understanding the substrate's own organization. Map correspondences between the five elements, five limbs, five sons, five garments, five senses, five trees, five fleshes, five fathers, etc. — they are not separate lists but restatements of one five-fold architecture at different scales. This pattern should guide restoration work: where a five-fold sequence is missing a member, that indicates either manuscript damage or over-stripping.

findings.title: Body-cosmos correspondence preserves proto-Indo-Iranian macrocosm-microcosm teaching
findings.current_state: §371: 'All the error, when the enemy of the lights constructed it, he constructed after the likeness of a man. The head of the universe is the beginning of the garments...'; §726: 'This whole universe, above and below, reflects the pattern of the human body'; §727: detailed mapping of body parts to cosmic structures; §754–§759: zodiac signs mapped onto body from head to feet.
findings.explanation: The systematic body-cosmos correspondence appears in three distinct passages (§371–§372, §726–§728, §742–§759), each providing a complete mapping between the human body and the cosmic order. This is one of the oldest layers visible in the substrate. The teaching that the cosmos is arranged after the pattern of the human form — and conversely that the human body mirrors the cosmic architecture — is a foundational Indo-Iranian doctrine attested in the Rigveda (Purusha Sukta, RV 10.90), in the Avestan Bundahišn (the cosmic body of Gayōmard), and in Mesopotamian traditions (the body of Tiamat as world-material). The three passages in the substrate represent three distinct applications: the inverted/evil cosmos (§371–§372), the regenerate/true cosmos (§726–§728), and the zodiacal body (§754–§759). The zodiacal body in §754–§759 is particularly archaic — it maps twelve cosmic principles to body regions in a system older than Greek zodiacal melothesia, possibly reflecting Mesopotamian astral-body correspondences.
findings.recommendation: Note as a deeper transmission layer. The body-cosmos correspondence predates the specifically Persian-Zoroastrian formulation and reaches back to proto-Indo-Iranian and Mesopotamian sources. Cross-reference with Rigvedic Purusha Sukta, Avestan Bundahišn Chapter 28 (the body of Gayōmard), and Babylonian astral-medical texts. The three distinct deployments should be studied as complementary perspectives on a single ancient teaching.

findings.title: Butter-in-milk analogy preserves a distinctly Indo-Iranian/Vedic teaching image
findings.current_state: §165: 'this counsel... resembles thus cooled butter. If a person will take and set it in hot milk, it melts down and soaks in with this hot milk. It melts in another time in silence and quiet to the midst of the milk... the oil and the grease and the beauty of the milk it shall gather in to it.'
findings.explanation: The extended analogy of butter placed in hot milk — dissolving into it silently, working from within to extract the good essence while discarding the impure — is a direct parallel to the Vedic/Upanishadic churning metaphor (cf. Rigveda 9.74.4, Śvetāśvatara Upanishad 1.15-16: 'As oil in sesame seeds, as butter in cream, as water in riverbeds... so is the Self seized in one's own self'). The image of extracting butter from milk is the quintessential Indo-Iranian metaphor for separating spirit from matter, divine essence from material admixture. Its presence in the substrate, as an extended and carefully developed analogy for how the divine counsel works silently within the mixed elements, strongly suggests that this passage preserves not just a Persian but a proto-Indo-Iranian teaching image. This is older than the Zoroastrian formulation.
findings.recommendation: Flag as deep transmission. This analogy may be the single clearest indicator of the substrate's Indo-Iranian (and possibly pre-Zoroastrian) heritage. Cross-reference with Vedic soma-churning texts and Upanishadic butter metaphors. The passage's teaching — that divine wisdom enters the mixed natural state, works in silence, and progressively extracts what is good while discarding what is impure — is itself a correspondential description of regeneration expressed through the most ancient available analogy.

findings.title: Five dark elements (smoke, fire, wind, water, darkness) preserve Zurvanite pre-Zoroastrian cosmology
findings.current_state: §48: 'Five storehouses have arisen since the beginning in the land of darkness! The five elements poured out of them... which are smoke, fire, wind, water and darkness'; §225: 'It generated itself of the five dark elements; which are smoke, fire, wind, water and Darkness.'
findings.explanation: The five dark elements — smoke, fire, wind, water, and darkness — form a consistent pentad throughout the corpus that does not correspond to any standard Greek or Zoroastrian elemental system. The standard Zoroastrian elements are fire, water, earth, air, plants, animals (or fire, water, earth, metal, plants). The standard Greek elements are earth, water, air, fire (plus aether). The substrate's five dark elements appear to preserve a Zurvanite or proto-Zurvanite cosmological system that predates the classical Zoroastrian formulation. 'Smoke' (= obscurity of understanding), 'fire' (= self-love), 'wind' (= persuasion/false reasoning), 'water' (= falsity proper), and 'darkness' (= total privation) form a phenomenological rather than physical elemental system — they describe modes of spiritual opposition rather than material substances. This suggests an older correspondential classification that the later Zoroastrian tradition modified into its physical element scheme.
findings.recommendation: Note as a deeper transmission layer. The five dark elements may preserve one of the oldest cosmological classification systems in the Ancient Word tradition — a correspondential pentad of spiritual evils predating both Greek and standard Zoroastrian elemental systems. Compare with the Bundahišn's account of Ahriman's five species of demons and with Zurvanite texts describing the five modes of evil. The consistent correspondential mapping (smoke = obscured understanding, fire = self-love, wind = false persuasion, water = flowing falsity, darkness = total privation) is remarkably precise and suggests a highly developed system of correspondences.

findings.title: Three great epochs structure spans two distinct chapters as a single teaching arc
findings.current_state: §167–§178 presents three 'seasons' (epochs) of cosmic history: (1) the First Man's descent and combat, (2) the Living Spirit's construction of the universe, (3) the Ambassador's manifestation through the Last Statue. §414–§428 presents 'three great days' and 'two deaths' that map onto the same tripartite structure: (1) the descent and rescue, (2) reign in the new aeon, (3) the Father's final unveiling.
findings.explanation: The three-epoch structure appears in two widely separated teaching units (§167–§178 and §414–§428) with different vocabulary but identical architecture. In §167–§178, the three are called 'seasons' (periods of time) and emphasize duration — the first is longest, the second shortest, the third intermediate. In §414–§428, the three are called 'days' and emphasize experiential quality — combat/affliction, reign/joy, unveiled divine presence. The two passages are complementary: one gives the temporal structure, the other the experiential content. This suggests they were originally parts of a single teaching about the three states of redemption, separated by the Manichaean compiler into different chapter locations. The correspondence between the two is visible only at corpus scale.
findings.recommendation: Note as a cross-passage structural pattern. The two passages should be read together as complementary views of a single three-epoch teaching. Consider whether the original substrate had these as a continuous sequence that the compiler separated.

findings.title: Four days / four nights / four hunters of light / four hunters of darkness form a single fourfold symmetry
findings.current_state: Four great days (§23–§28), four great nights (§29–§38), four hunters of light (§39–§43), four hunters of darkness (§44–§47) — all presented as parallel tetrads within a single chapter.
findings.explanation: This teaching unit presents four parallel fourfold structures that mirror each other precisely: the four days describe four states of divine illumination; the four nights describe four corresponding states of spiritual darkness; the four hunters of light describe four active divine operations; the four hunters of darkness describe four corresponding infernal operations. The symmetry is exact — each divine state has its infernal counterpart, each active divine operation has its infernal mirror. This grand fourfold symmetry is the substrate's way of teaching that the entire spiritual world is organized in corresponding pairs of good and evil, light and darkness, at every scale. The four-fold pattern here complements the five-fold pattern seen elsewhere — four representing correspondence/symmetry, five representing discrete degrees.
findings.recommendation: Note as a foundational structural pattern. The four-fold symmetry (day/night, hunter/counter-hunter) operates as the substrate's principal means of teaching about correspondences between states of good and states of evil. This complements the five-fold pattern (which teaches about discrete degrees of the divine proceeding). Together, the four and the five constitute the substrate's complete structural vocabulary.

findings.title: Twelve-fold completeness structures span multiple chapters as a unified doctrine of total spiritual order
findings.current_state: Twelve judges (§283–§296), eighteen thrones (§297–§314), twelve seals on the wheel (§356–§361), twelve zodiacal signs assigned to five dark worlds (§713–§725), twelve signs mapped to the body (§754–§759).
findings.explanation: The number twelve functions throughout the corpus as a marker of completeness — specifically, the completeness of all goods and truths (or all evils and falsities) in their total arrangement. The twelve judges represent the complete system of divine discernment; the twelve seals represent the complete restraining order of Providence; the twelve zodiacal rulers represent the complete system of falsity from evil. Each twelve-fold structure deploys differently but expresses the same principle: that spiritual reality, whether divine or infernal, organizes itself into a complete circle of twelve fundamental states. This maps precisely to Swedenborg's teaching that twelve signifies 'all things of faith and the church in their completeness' (AC 577, 3272, 3858). The substrate's twelve-fold structures are never arbitrary lists but always complete systems — the full circle of spiritual states in a given domain.
findings.recommendation: Treat the twelve-fold structures as expressions of a single substrate doctrine about spiritual completeness. Map correspondences between the different twelve-fold systems — they should illuminate each other as different perspectives on the same complete order.

findings.title: Marsh/fish imagery and ship-through-water analogy preserve pre-Persian teaching images
findings.current_state: §566: 'Just like a marsh, of which the fish and birds are snared in a net, and only the waters are left behind and the reeds and the plants that grow in it'; §543: 'the conduits are like the waters through which ships sail... immediately and without delay the waters mingle with each other again behind the ship; and the path of the ship shall not be discernible in the midst of the waters'
findings.explanation: Two teaching images in the substrate resist identification with specifically Persian cultural vocabulary and point to an older, possibly Mesopotamian transmission layer. The marsh image in §566 — a stagnant wetland from which living things are extracted while reeds and water remain — is a distinctly riverine/Mesopotamian image. The ship-through-water analogy in §543–§545, teaching that spiritual influx passes through truth without disrupting or leaving a trace (as a ship passes through water), is a remarkably precise correspondential image about the nature of spiritual substance. The teaching that 'the path of the ship shall not be discernible in the midst of the waters' — that influx leaves no trace in the medium it passes through — expresses a principle about the relationship between spiritual and natural substance that is prior to any specific cultural formulation.
findings.recommendation: Note as potential Mesopotamian or proto-Indo-Iranian transmission. The marsh image in particular suggests a southern Mesopotamian (Sumerian/Babylonian) cultural setting — the marshlands of southern Iraq where both Manichaean communities and pre-Zoroastrian Iranian traditions had deep roots. The ship-through-water analogy may be one of the oldest surviving correspondential images about the nature of spiritual influx.

findings.title: Abrupt exclamatory transition at §7 suggests missing connective material
findings.current_state: §7: 'Then the Third Ambassador! [He purified the light] by his image. He became [redeemer of] all things.'
findings.explanation: §7 introduces the Third Ambassador with an exclamation ('Then the Third Ambassador!') that feels abrupt after the preceding cosmogonic narrative of §1–§6. The exclamation mark (likely reflecting an emphatic particle in the Coptic) and the extremely compressed description (a single sentence covering the entire third cosmogonic act) contrast sharply with the more developed accounts in §4–§6. This may indicate either (a) the extraction pipeline removed introductory material that connected §6 to §7 more smoothly, or (b) manuscript damage compressed what was originally a more developed passage, or (c) the substrate itself used a telegraphic style for this transition. Given that the Third Ambassador receives extensive treatment elsewhere in the corpus (§25, §41, §67, §69, §113, §143, §156–§159, §171–§172, etc.), the extreme brevity here is noteworthy and may indicate over-stripping of explanatory material.
findings.recommendation: Investigate whether the extraction pipeline removed material between §6 and §7, or between §7 and §8, that originally developed the Third Ambassador's cosmogonic role more fully. Compare with the parallel account in §171 which provides a much more developed narrative of the same event.

summary.overall_assessment: The extraction is generally well-executed — the substrate teaching flows coherently across chapters, and the five-fold, four-fold, and twelve-fold architectures emerge clearly at corpus scale. The most serious issues are naming overlays rather than extraction errors. The 'Jesus' prefix on cosmic entities (Splendour, Youth) is the single most consequential overlay, affecting 15+ passages and obscuring the substrate's own Persian designation for these figures. 'Saklas' (Gnostic), 'Matter/Hylē' (Greek philosophical), 'Cross of Light/crucified' (Christian-Manichaean), 'Holy Spirit' (Christian), and 'second death' (Revelation) represent additional layers of editorial vocabulary that survived extraction. The substrate itself — visible through all these overlays — preserves a remarkably coherent five-fold correspondential system that maps divine proceeding, human faculties, cosmic structure, and infernal opposition onto a single architectural template. The deeper transmission layers (Indo-Iranian butter-in-milk, Zurvanite five dark elements, proto-Mesopotamian marsh imagery) confirm that the substrate carries material older than the specifically Persian-Zoroastrian formulation.
summary.extraction_assessment: The pipeline tends slightly toward under-stripping rather than over-stripping. The clearest residual editorial items are 'Holy Spirit' (§427, §617), 'second death' (§428), 'the elect one' (§106, §413), 'church tutelaries' (§95), and the audience frame in §577. These are Christian and Manichaean institutional/theological terms that slipped through extraction because they were embedded within otherwise substrate passages. The single possible case of over-stripping is at §7, where the Third Ambassador's cosmogonic role is compressed to a single sentence — but this could equally be manuscript damage. No chapter shows systematic over-stripping.
